Whereto
whair-TOO
adv.
From where and to: to which; to what end. Webster 1828: to which; to what. Isaiah uses it for the errand on which God sends His word, and Paul for the point a believer has already reached.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The great promise about the effectiveness of God’s word turns on this word, and the promise is about an errand rather than a result in general: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it (Isaiah 55:11). The word is not guaranteed to do whatever the preacher hoped; it is guaranteed to accomplish what God sent it to do, which in the same chapter includes hardening as well as blessing. Paul uses it of the ground already gained: Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing (Philippians 3:16). Christians will not all be at the same point, and Paul’s rule is that each walk by what he has been given rather than dispute about the rest. He uses it again in one of the New Testament’s most compact statements of conversion: ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you (Romans 6:17). Job uses it in bitter interrogation: whereto might the strength of their hands profit me, in whom old age was perished? (Job 30:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WHERETO as to which; to what; and in older usage, to what end or purpose.

expand to see more

WHERETO, adv. — To which; as, the end whereto he was appointed.

To what; to what end; as, whereto serveth this?

Compare WHEREUNTO, of the same sense and more frequent in the Authorized Version.

Compare WHEREFORE, for which cause; WHEREBY, by which means.

From where and to.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Philippians 3:16 — "Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing."

Romans 6:17 — "But God be thanked, that ye were the servants of sin, but ye have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered you."

Job 30:2 — "Yea, whereto might the strength of their hands profit me, in whom old age was perished?"

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 55:11 promises that God’s word accomplishes God’s purpose, not the preacher’s, and it is commonly quoted as though it guaranteed visible success for every sermon.

expand to see more

It shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it. The guarantee is tied to God’s errand, and Isaiah’s own commission earlier in the book shows how wide that errand runs: he is sent to a people whose ears will be made heavy and whose eyes will be shut (Isaiah 6:9-10), and our Lord applies the same passage to His own hearers. The word never returns void, but its non-void effect may be hardening as truly as saving — Paul says the gospel is a savour of death unto death in them that perish and of life unto life in them that are saved (2 Corinthians 2:15-16). Preachers who quote Isaiah 55:11 to guarantee visible fruit have narrowed the promise and set themselves up for a discouragement the text does not require. The faithful man’s comfort is that the errand is God’s and the accomplishment is certain, whatever he can see of it.

Philippians 3:16 is a rule for peace among believers who are not at the same place, and it is easy to abuse in either direction. Paul has just said he does not count himself to have apprehended, and he allows that God will reveal to some what they do not yet see; his instruction is that each walk by what he has attained rather than break fellowship over the remainder. That is not a warrant for doctrinal indifference — the same epistle is fierce about the concision and about enemies of the cross, and the same apostle wrote Galatians. The distinction is the one the Reformers made between fundamental articles and matters of lesser weight, and keeping it is the difference between a church that can hold together and a movement that fractures over every disagreement.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asher... lo, that to which; tsalach (H6743), to prosper or succeed; Greek eis ho, unto which; phthano (G5348), to arrive at, to attain.

expand to see more

Hebrew asher shalach — that to which He sent it; the errand clause of Isaiah 55:11.

Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to push forward, to prosper, to succeed in a purpose (Isaiah 55:11).

Hebrew reyqam (H7387) — empty, void, without effect; what the word shall not be.

Greek phthano (G5348) — to arrive at, to attain; whereto we have already attained (Philippians 3:16).

Greek tupos (G5179) — a form, mould or pattern; the form of doctrine delivered in Romans 6:17.

Usage

"It shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it (Isaiah 55:11) — the guarantee is tied to God’s errand, not the preacher’s hope."

"Whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule (Philippians 3:16) — a rule for believers not at the same place."

"That form of doctrine which was delivered you (Romans 6:17) — the mould into which the converted are poured."
